content.title: About
content.content: Canned asparagus cooked in vegetable oil consists of selected asparagus spears that are peeled, blanched and packed in glass or metal jars with added oil. The product is ready to eat and retains the characteristic aroma, a pleasant bite and the nutritional qualities of fresh asparagus.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Asparagus has been cultivated for more than 2,000 years, dating back to ancient Egypt and Rome.
Canning extends the shelf life to 2–3 years while preserving flavor and nutrients.
The oil (often olive or sunflower) enhances taste and improves absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.
Heat treatment increases the concentration of aromatic compounds that give asparagus its distinctive scent.
In many countries canned asparagus is a popular ingredient in salads, appetizers and as a side dish for meat.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Source of folate
items.content: Folate (vitamin B9) supports cell division and is especially important during pregnancy.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Asparagus provides glutathione, vitamin C and carotenoids that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: One cup of canned asparagus (≈150 g) contains about 30 kcal, making it a diet‑friendly food.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps maintain satiety.

items.title: Allergy to amaranth family vegetables
items.content: A small number of people may experience an allergic reaction to asparagus.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Canned foods often contain added salt; those monitoring sodium intake should account for it.

items.title: Oil content
items.content: The added oil increases the caloric density; portion control is advisable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Bacterial safety
items.content: Damaged cans (dents, bulging) may compromise safety and should be discarded.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Canned asparagus can be eaten straight from the jar, added to salads, pastas, omelets, or used in hot dishes such as stews and casseroles. It is often briefly warmed in a skillet with a little extra oil before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened jars in a cool, dry place away from direct light. After opening, transfer the asparagus to an airtight container and keep it refrigerated for 3–4 days. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Light beer is a fermented beverage made from malted barley, hops, water and yeast. It has a pale golden colour, moderate bitterness and a hop‑forward aroma with hints of fruit and grain. Typical alcohol content ranges from 4% to 5%.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Light beer is often referred to as a “lager”, although lagers can also be dark.
The first modern light beer was brewed in Bavaria in the 19th century.
Hops act as a natural preservative, extending the shelf life of the beer.
Different countries have their own traditional names for light beer: “Pilsner” in the Czech Republic, “Pale Ale” in the UK.
Light beer is usually served chilled at 4–7 °C.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Beer provides B1, B2, B6 and folate, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Beneficial polyphenols
items.content: Hops and malt contain antioxidant polyphenols that may protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: May support cardiovascular health
items.content: Moderate consumption of light beer has been linked to higher levels of “good” HDL cholesterol.

items.title: Provides minerals
items.content: Beer contains potassium, magnesium and phosphorus, essential for muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: Malt supplies dietary fiber that can help maintain regular bowel movements.

items.title: Alcohol content
items.content: Beer contains alcohol, so it should be consumed in moderation and avoided during pregnancy, while driving, or by people with liver disease.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Light beer provides about 40–45 kcal per 100 ml, which can contribute to weight gain if consumed in excess.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Barley malt contains gluten, making beer unsuitable for individuals with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Hops allergy
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to hops.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve light beer chilled in a 300–500 ml glass or mug. It pairs well with light snacks such as nuts, cheese, fish, grilled chicken or salads.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store beer in a dark, cool place at 7–12 °C. Once opened, reseal the bottle and consume within 2–3 days to preserve flavor and aroma.
